questions.q: What is the genre of "On the Face of It" and who is the author?
questions.a: The genre is a one-act play (drama) and the author is Susan Hill. A wrong answer (e.g., "short story" or "poem") reveals the student cannot distinguish dramatic form from narrative prose, which will hinder understanding of stage directions, dialogue-driven characterisation, and the immediate, present-tense experience of a play.

questions.q: In your own words, explain the central question posed in the "Before you read" box and why it is important for reading the play.
questions.a: The central question is: "What is the bond that unites the two?" (the old man and the boy). It is important because it gives a specific lens — look for moments of connection, shared experience, or mutual understanding — rather than just following the plot. A wrong answer that merely summarises the plot ("an old man meets a boy in a garden") shows the student is reading for events, not for the thematic relationship the question directs them to find.

questions.q: Based on the "Before you read" box, list three specific details about the setting and the two main characters that you would expect to see developed in the play.
questions.a: Setting: Mr Lamb's garden (outdoors, natural, accessible). Character 1: Mr Lamb — old man, has a tin leg (lost real leg), lives alone in a big house. Character 2: Derry — 14-year-old boy, withdrawn and defiant, has a burned face (acid injury). A wrong answer that omits the tin leg or the burned face misses the physical impairments that drive the play's exploration of alienation vs. connection.

questions.q: Compare the description of Derry in the "Before you read" box ("very withdrawn and defiant") with the actual opening dialogue in Scene One (Derry's first words: "What? Who's that? Who's there?" and "I thought this was an empty place."). What does this comparison reveal about how the pre-reading context prepares (or fails to prepare) the reader?
questions.a: The pre-reading label "withdrawn and defiant" is an interpretive summary, while the dialogue shows Derry's immediate panic and fear ("Panic" stage direction) and his assumption of emptiness. The comparison reveals that the pre-reading box gives a thematic label (defiant) that the text initially contradicts with vulnerability (fear). A student who expects only defiance will misread Derry's opening fear as aggression; the pre-reading context must be held lightly and tested against the text.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The 'Before you read' box tells us the play is about disability." Is this claim accurate, partially accurate, or inaccurate? Justify using only the information in the box.
questions.a: Partially accurate. The box mentions physical impairments (tin leg, burned face) and the boy's withdrawal/defiance, but the central question asks about the "bond that unites the two," not about disability per se. The play uses disability as a circumstance to explore human connection and alienation. A student who says "accurate" will read reductively, looking only for disability tropes; a student who says "inaccurate" misses that the impairments are the catalyst for the alienation the bond must overcome.

questions.q: Write a new "Before you read" box for a modern Indian adaptation of this play. Keep the same structure: genre, author (you), setting, two characters with contrasting physical/social differences, and one central question about their bond.
questions.a: Example: "This is a one-act play by [Student Name]. It features a retired army officer who uses a wheelchair and a teenage girl who stutters severely, meeting in the officer's rooftop garden in Delhi. The officer loves growing bonsai; the girl skips school to avoid oral exams. What is the bond that unites them?" A poor answer would copy the original characters or omit the central question, showing the student hasn't internalised the function of a pre-reading frame.
